When the seven awakening factors are developed and cultivated in this way they can expect seven fruits and benefits.
What seven?
They attain enlightenment early on in this very life.
If not, they attain enlightenment at the time of death.
If not, with the ending of the five lower fetters, they’re extinguished between one life and the next.
If not, with the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished upon landing.
If not, with the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished without extra effort.
If not, with the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished with extra effort.
If not, with the ending of the five lower fetters they head upstream, going to the Akaniṭṭha realm.
When the seven awakening factors are developed and cultivated in this way these are the seven fruits and benefits they can expect.”

These ten things, monks, are desired, loved, and agreeable, but are difficult to obtain in the world.

3. Regarding these ten things, monks, which are desired, loved, agreeable, and difficult to obtain in the world, there are ten obstacles <term>paripanthā</term> <gloss>impediments or dangers that block the way</gloss>:

4. Laziness and lack of effort are the obstacle to wealth. Lack of grooming and lack of adornment are the obstacle to physical beauty. Engaging in unsuitable habits is the obstacle to health. Evil friendship is the obstacle to virtuous conduct. Lack of sense restraint is the obstacle to the holy life <term>brahmacariya</term> <gloss>the path of purity or celibacy</gloss>. Deception is the obstacle to friendships. Lack of recitation is the obstacle to great learning. Lack of desire to listen and lack of questioning are the obstacle to wisdom. Lack of application and lack of reflection are the obstacle to understanding the teachings <term>dhammānam</term>. Wrong practice is the obstacle to the heavenly realms.

These, monks, are the ten obstacles to those ten things that are desired, loved, agreeable, and difficult to obtain in the world.

5. Regarding these ten things, monks, which are desired, loved, agreeable, and difficult to obtain in the world, there are ten nourishments <term>āhārā</term> <gloss>supporting conditions or fuels</gloss>:

6. Diligence and effort are the nourishment for wealth. Grooming and adornment are the nourishment for physical beauty. Engaging in suitable habits is the nourishment for health. Good friendship is the nourishment for virtuous conduct. Sense restraint is the nourishment for the holy life. Honesty is the nourishment for friendships. Recitation is the nourishment for great learning. The desire to listen and frequent questioning are the nourishment for wisdom. Constant application and reflection are the nourishment for understanding the teachings. Right practice is the nourishment for the heavenly realms.

These, monks, are the ten nourishments for those ten things that are desired, loved, agreeable, and difficult to obtain in the world.

These, monks, are the ten sustaining conditions for these ten things that are desirable, pleasing, agreeable, and rare in the world.

Pañca kho ime, māṇava, nīvaraṇā. Katame pañca? — Kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ vyāpādanīvaraṇaṃ thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ¹ uddhaccakukkuccanīvaraṇaṃ vicikicchānīvaraṇaṃ. Ime kho, māṇava, pañca nīvaraṇā. Imehi kho, māṇava, pañcahi² nīvaraṇehi brāhmaṇo Pokkharasāti Opamañño Subhagavaniko āvaṭo³ nivuṭo ophiṭo⁴ pariyonaddho. So vata uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ ñassati vā dakkhiti vā sacchi vā karissatīti, — n’ etaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Pañca kho ime, māṇava, kāmaguṇā. Katame pañca? — Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā⁵ sotaviññeyyā saddā, —pe— ghānaviññeyyā gandhā, jivhāviññeyyā rasā, kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā⁶ iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Ime kho, māṇava, pañca kāmaguṇā. Imehi kho⁷, māṇava, pañcahi⁸ kāmaguṇehi brāhmaṇo Pokkharasāti Opamañño Subhagavaniko gathito⁹ mucchito ajjhopanno anādinavadassāvī anissaraṇapañño paribhuñjati. So vata uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ ñassati vā dakkhiti vā sacchi vā karissatīti, — n’ etaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, māṇava? Yaṃ vā tiṇakaṭṭhupādānaṃ paṭicca aggiṃ jāleyya¹⁰, yaṃ vā nissaṭṭhatiṇakaṭṭhupādānaṃ aggiṃ¹¹ jāleyya, — katamo nu khvassa aggi accimā ca¹² vaṇṇimā ca pabhassaro cāti?

Sace taṃ, bho Gotama, ṭhānaṃ¹³ nissaṭṭhatiṇakaṭṭhupādānaṃ aggiṃ jālitum¹⁴, svāssa aggi accimā ca vaṇṇimā ca pabhassaro cāti.

Aṭṭhānaṃ kho etaṃ, māṇava, anavakāso, yaṃ nissaṭṭhatiṇakaṭṭhupādānaṃ aggiṃ jāleyya¹⁵ aññatra iddhimatā. Seyyathāpi, māṇava, tiṇakaṭṭhupādānaṃ¹⁶ paṭicca aggi¹⁷ jalati, tathūpamāhaṃ, māṇava, imaṃ pītiṃ vadāmi, yāyaṃ pīti

---

“Student, there are these five hindrances.
What five?
The hindrances of sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
These are the five hindrances.
Pokkharasāti is obstructed, hindered, engulfed, and enveloped by these five hindrances.
It is quite impossible for him to know or see or realize a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
There are these five kinds of sensual stimulation.
What five?
There are sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.
There are sounds known by the ear …
smells known by the nose …
tastes known by the tongue …
touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.
These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation.
Pokkharasāti enjoys these five kinds of sensual stimulation, tied, infatuated, attached, blind to the drawbacks, and not understanding the escape.
It is quite impossible for him to know or see or realize a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
What do you think, student?
Which would have better flames, color, and radiance: a fire that depends on grass and logs as fuel, or one that does not?”
“If it were possible for a fire to burn without depending on grass and logs as fuel, that would have better flames, color, and radiance.”
“But it isn’t possible, except by psychic power.
Rapture that depends on the five kinds of sensual stimulation is like a fire that depends on grass and logs as fuel.
Rapture that’s apart from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities is like a fire that doesn’t depend on grass and logs as fuel.
[context] And what is rapture that’s apart from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities?
[context] It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.
[context] This is rapture that’s apart from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities.

### 9. Discourse to Subha (99)

Young man, there are these five <term>nīvaraṇā</term> <gloss>hindrances</gloss>. Which five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill-will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. These, young man, are the five hindrances. By these five hindrances, the Brahmin <note>a member of the priestly caste</note> Pokkharasāti Opamañño of Subhaga Grove is obstructed, secluded, blocked, and enveloped. That he should know or see or realize any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones—this is impossible.

Young man, there are these five <term>kāmaguṇā</term> <gloss>strands of sensual pleasure</gloss>. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, likeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. Sounds cognizable by the ear... odors cognizable by the nose... flavors cognizable by the tongue... touches cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable, likeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. These, young man, are the five strands of sensual pleasure. With these five strands of sensual pleasure, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti Opamañño of Subhaga Grove is tied, infatuated, and obsessed; he enjoys them without seeing the danger or knowing the escape. That he should know or see or realize any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones—this is impossible.

What do you think, young man? Suppose someone were to kindle a fire depending on grass and wood as fuel, and another person were to kindle a fire without any grass or wood as fuel. Which of these two fires would have flame, color, and radiance?

If it were possible, Master Gotama, to kindle a fire without any grass or wood as fuel, that fire would have flame, color, and radiance.

Young man, it is impossible, there is no way, that a fire could be kindled without grass or wood as fuel, except by one with psychic power. Just as a fire burns depending on grass and wood as fuel, even so, young man, do I describe this rapture—that <term>pīti</term> <gloss>rapture</gloss> which...

<summary>The Buddha explains to the young man Subha how the five hindrances and five strands of sensual pleasure prevent spiritual realization. He uses an analogy of a fire requiring fuel to illustrate the nature of worldly rapture compared to spiritual attainment.</summary>

5. 9. SUBHASUTTAM (99).

These five, young man, are the hindrances. Which five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill-will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and worry, and the hindrance of doubt. These, young man, are the five hindrances. By these five hindrances, the brahmin Pokkharasāti of the Opamañña clan, a resident of Subhaga, is obstructed, hindered, covered, and enveloped. That he should know, see, or realize a state of super-human knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones—such a thing cannot happen.

These five, young man, are the strands of sensual pleasure. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, pleasant, agreeable, attractive, associated with sensual desire, and stimulating; sounds cognizable by the ear; <note>etc.</note> odors cognizable by the nose; flavors cognizable by the tongue; and tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, pleasant, agreeable, attractive, associated with sensual desire, and stimulating. These, young man, are the five strands of sensual pleasure. By these five strands of sensual pleasure, the brahmin Pokkharasāti of the Opamañña clan, a resident of Subhaga, is bound, infatuated, attached, not seeing the danger, and lacking the wisdom of escape, as he enjoys them. That he should know, see, or realize a state of super-human knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones—such a thing cannot happen.

If, Master Gotama, one were able to kindle a fire without depending on grass and wood, that would be the fire that is radiant, colorful, and brilliant.

That is an impossible state, young man, a situation that cannot occur, that one could kindle a fire without depending on grass and wood, unless one were a person of psychic power. # The Octad Chapter <note>original: "Atthakavagga"</note>

836. <note>Māgandiya speaks:</note> "If you do not desire such a jewel, a woman sought after by many lords of men, then what kind of doctrine do you proclaim, regarding views, lives led according to habitual moral vows, and rebirth in future existences?"

837. <note>The Blessed One <gloss>Bhagavā</gloss> speaks:</note> "Māgandiya," said the Blessed One, "the thought 'I proclaim this' does not occur to the one who has reached a conclusion after grasping among doctrines. Looking among various views and not grasping them, I saw and searched for inner peace <note>original: "ajjhattasanti"</note>."

838. <note>Māgandiya speaks:</note> "O Sage <gloss>muni</gloss>," said Māgandiya, "you speak of not grasping those conclusions that have been constructed. This matter called 'inner peace,' how is that explained by the wise?"

839. <note>The Blessed One speaks:</note> "Māgandiya," said the Blessed One, "one does not speak of purity <gloss>suddhim</gloss> through views, nor through learning, nor through knowledge, nor even through habitual moral vows. Nor is purity achieved through lack of views, lack of learning, lack of knowledge, or lack of vows. Having abandoned these without grasping, being peaceful and independent, one would not long for becoming <note>original: "bhavaṃ," referring to future existence or rebirth</note>."

840. <note>Māgandiya speaks:</note> "If, as you say, one does not speak of purity through views, nor through learning, nor through knowledge, nor even through habitual moral vows..."

<summary>The Brahmin Māgandiya questions the Buddha on how purity and inner peace are attained if not through traditional religious vows or intellectual views. The Buddha explains that true peace comes from non-attachment to all views and future existences.</summary>
<keywords>Magandiya Sutta, Atthakavagga, inner peace, views, purity, non-attachment, rebirth, Buddhist philosophy</keywords>

837. "There is no 'this is what I maintain' for him," said the Blessed One, "O Māgandiya, among things grasped by determination. Seeing no support in views, he seeks internal peace, having seen through <note>the nature of</note> it."

838. "Those determinations that have been fabricated," said Māgandiya, "you speak of those indeed as without support, O Sage. How is this meaning of 'internal peace' explained by the wise?"

839. "Not by view, not by tradition, not by knowledge," said the Blessed One, "O Māgandiya, nor by virtuous conduct and rites does one say purity is attained. Neither by view, nor by tradition, nor by knowledge, nor by lack of view, lack of tradition, nor lack of knowledge, nor by lack of virtuous conduct, nor by lack of rites, is it attained. Relinquishing these and not grasping, being at peace, one does not long for existence."

21. Then Craving <term>Taṇhā</term>, Discontent <term>Arati</term>, and Passion <term>Ragā</term>, the daughters of Mara, approached Mara the Evil One.

22. Mara the Evil One saw Craving, Discontent, and Passion, his daughters, coming from afar. Seeing them, he addressed them in verses:

Fools! You try to crush a mountain with the stalks of water lilies.
You dig into a mountain with your fingernails. You chew iron with your teeth.
As if lifting a rock with your head, you seek a foothold in the abyss.
As if attacking a tree stump with your chest, you go away frustrated by Gotama.

23. Blazing with beauty they came: Craving, Discontent, and Passion.

[context] What four?
[context] One thunders but doesn’t rain,
[context] one rains but doesn’t thunder,
one neither thunders nor rains, and
one both rains and thunders.
These are the four kinds of clouds.
In the same way, these four individuals similar to clouds are found in the world.
What four?
One thunders but doesn’t rain,
one rains but doesn’t thunder,
one neither thunders nor rains, and
one both rains and thunders.
And how does an individual thunder but not rain?
It’s when an individual memorizes the teaching—
statements, mixed prose & verse, discussions, verses, inspired exclamations, legends, stories of past lives, amazing stories, and elaborations.
But they don’t truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.
That’s how an individual thunders but doesn’t rain.
That individual is like a cloud that thunders but doesn’t rain, I say.
And how does an individual rain but not thunder?
It’s when an individual doesn’t memorize the teaching …
But they truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ …
And how does an individual neither thunder nor rain?
It’s when an individual doesn’t memorize the teaching …
Nor do they truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ …
And how does an individual both thunder and rain?
It’s when an individual memorizes the teaching …
And they truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ …
[context] These four individuals similar to clouds are found in the world.”

# THE CLOUD CHAPTER <note>original: Valāhakavagga</note>

102.

1. Monks <note>original: bhikkhave</note>, there are these four types of clouds. Which four?
The one that thunders but does not rain <note>original: gajjitā no vassitā</note>... <note>the text elides the intermediate types here</note> ...and the one that both thunders and rains.
These, monks, are the four types of clouds.

2. In the same way, monks, these four people who resemble clouds are found existing in the world. Which four?
The one who thunders but does not rain... and the one who both thunders and rains.

3. And how, monks, is a person one who thunders but does not rain?
In this case, monks, a certain person masters the Teaching <note>original: dhammam</note>, namely: the discourses <note>original: suttam</note>, the mixed prose and verse <note>original: geyyam</note>, the explanations <note>original: veyyākaraṇam</note>, the verses <note>original: gātham</note>, the inspired utterances <note>original: udānam</note>, the "as it was said" quotations <note>original: itivuttakam</note>, the birth stories <note>original: jātakam</note>, the marvelous qualities <note>original: abbhutadhammam</note>, and the interpretations <note>original: vedallam</note>. Yet he does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering" <note>original: dukkhan</note>... <note>the text elides the second and third truths</note> ...he does not understand as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering" <note>original: dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā</note>.
Thus, monks, a person is one who thunders but does not rain. I say this person is like that cloud which thunders but does not rain.

4. And how, monks, is a person one who rains but does not thunder?
In this case, monks, a certain person does not master the Teaching, namely: the discourses... the interpretations. Yet he understands as it really is: "This is suffering"... he understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering." Thus, monks, a person is one who rains but does not thunder. I say this person is like that [cloud]...

5. And how, monks, is a person one who neither thunders nor rains?
In this case, monks, a certain person does not master the Teaching, namely: the discourses... the interpretations. He does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering"... he does not understand as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering." Thus, monks, a person is one who neither thunders nor rains. I say this person is like that [cloud]...

6. And how, monks, is a person one who both thunders and rains?
In this case, monks, a certain person masters the Teaching, namely: the discourses... the interpretations. He understands as it really is: "This is suffering"... he understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering." Thus, monks, a person is one who both thunders and rains. Just as that cloud, monks, both thunders and rains, I say this person is like that.

<summary>The Buddha uses a metaphor of four types of clouds to categorize individuals based on their theoretical knowledge of the scriptures versus their actual realization of the Four Noble Truths.</summary>

VALĀHAKAVAGGA. 103

1. These four, monks, are clouds. Which four? 
Those that thunder but do not rain... (and so on)... and those that both thunder and rain. 
These, monks, are the four types of clouds.

2. Just so, monks, these four individuals like unto clouds are found in the world. Which four? 
Those that thunder but do not rain... (and so on)... and those that both thunder and rain.

3. And how, monks, is an individual like a cloud that thunders but does not rain? 
Here, monks, a certain individual learns the <term>Dhamma</term> <gloss>teaching</gloss>: discourses, songs, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, legendary tales, birth stories, marvelous events, and analytical descriptions. Yet, he does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering"... (and so on)... he does not understand as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, an individual is one who thunders but does not rain. Just as that cloud, monks, thunders but does not rain, so do I compare this individual to it.

4. And how, monks, is an individual like a cloud that rains but does not thunder? 
Here, monks, a certain individual does not learn the <term>Dhamma</term>: discourses... (and so on)... analytical descriptions. Yet, he understands as it really is: "This is suffering"... (and so on)... he understands as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, an individual is one who rains but does not thunder. Just as that cloud, monks... I compare him to it.

5. And how, monks, is an individual like a cloud that neither thunders nor rains? 
Here, monks, a certain individual does not learn the <term>Dhamma</term>: discourses... analytical descriptions. Furthermore, he does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering"... he does not understand as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, an individual is one who neither thunders nor rains. Just as that cloud, monks... I compare him to it.

6. And how, monks, is an individual like a cloud that both thunders and rains? 
Here, monks, a certain individual learns the <term>Dhamma</term>: discourses... analytical descriptions. Furthermore, he understands as it really is: "This is suffering"... he understands as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, an individual is one who both thunders and rains. Just as that cloud, monks, both thunders and rains, so do I compare this individual to it.
